trails.trailTip: Start early in summer — this trail has little shade and is one of the park's most popular, so the small trailhead lot fills quickly.
trails.didYouKnow: Hickman Bridge is a true natural bridge carved by flowing water, not an arch, spanning 133 feet.

trails.trailTip: Cairns mark the route across open slickrock, with real exposure near the arch itself — watch your footing and stay back from the unfenced edge above the span.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail and arch are named for outlaw Butch Cassidy, said to have used the area's canyons as a hideout.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; avoid if flash flood risk is present
trails.trailTip: Never enter this narrow-walled wash if rain is forecast anywhere upstream — per NPS guidance, flash floods here can arrive with little warning even from storms many miles away.
trails.didYouKnow: The Pioneer Register along this walk preserves names carved into the canyon wall by Mormon settlers and other travelers dating back to the 1870s.

trails.trailTip: The initial climb is steep and exposed to sun and wind — bring layers even in cooler months since the ridge offers little shelter.
trails.didYouKnow: Chimney Rock is a resistant sandstone spire capped by darker Moenkopi shale, left standing as softer rock eroded away around it.

trails.trailTip: The steep switchback start is the toughest part of the hike — pace yourself there and the trail eases once you're inside the canyon.
trails.didYouKnow: Cohab Canyon's name references 'cohabitation' — polygamist Mormon settlers reportedly hid here from federal marshals.

trails.trailTip: This is the park's most demanding maintained day hike — carry at least 3 liters of water and start early to avoid exposed slickrock in full summer heat.
trails.didYouKnow: Navajo Knobs offers a rare 360-degree view taking in the Waterpocket Fold, the Henry Mountains, and Capitol Dome.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; avoid if flash flood risk is present
trails.trailTip: Check the weather and ask a ranger about current wash conditions before hiking — this route follows a narrow drainage where flash floods, even from distant storms, are a real hazard.
trails.didYouKnow: Grand Wash narrows to as little as 20 feet wide between towering sandstone walls at its tightest point.

trails.bestSeason: Apr-Oct; avoid if flash flood risk is present
trails.trailTip: This route involves wading and scrambling through the creek itself with no maintained tread — check current conditions at the visitor center and never start if rain is forecast anywhere in the drainage.
trails.didYouKnow: Sulphur Creek passes three small waterfalls and slot sections not found on the park's maintained trail system, though it isn't an official maintained trail.

animals.whereToLook: Historic Fruita orchards and along the Fremont River
animals.viewingTip: Deer graze right in the historic orchards — enjoy watching from the orchard paths but don't approach closely or offer them fallen fruit.
animals.didYouKnow: Deer are drawn to Fruita's century-old orchards, which the park still maintains and lets visitors pick from in season.

animals.whereToLook: Steep canyon walls within the Waterpocket Fold
animals.viewingTip: Spot bighorn on distant canyon walls with binoculars rather than trying to close the distance over loose talus.
animals.didYouKnow: Desert bighorn were reintroduced to Capitol Reef after being extirpated in the early 20th century.

animals.whereToLook: Sandstone cliffs above the Fremont River
animals.viewingTip: Watch nesting cliffs from below with binoculars or a spotting scope rather than climbing toward a ledge for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: A stooping peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, exceeding 200 mph.

animals.viewingTip: Photograph basking lizards with a zoom lens from a few feet away instead of cornering them for a closer shot.
animals.didYouKnow: Male collared lizards turn vivid green and blue during breeding season to attract mates.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky canyon walls and near historic Fruita buildings after dark
animals.viewingTip: Ringtails are almost entirely nocturnal and rarely seen — if you spot one at night, keep a headlamp dim and don't try to approach or feed it.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the nickname 'ringtail cat,' ringtails are actually related to raccoons, not cats.

animals.whereToLook: Thermals above the reef's sandstone cliffs
animals.viewingTip: Scan cliff faces and the sky with binoculars from pullouts rather than approaching a cliff base where a nest might be.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles build massive stick nests they reuse and add to for years, sometimes weighing hundreds of pounds.

animals.whereToLook: Cottonwoods in the historic orchard area
animals.viewingTip: If you spot one resting in a tree, view it from the ground with binoculars — never touch or try to move a porcupine, since their barbed quills detach and work deeper into flesh once embedded.
animals.didYouKnow: Porcupine quills have microscopic barbs that make them work deeper into flesh once embedded, so hikers and pets should keep well clear.

animals.whereToLook: Around the historic orchard and campground area
animals.viewingTip: Rock squirrels are used to people and will approach on their own — don't feed them, since human food and close contact make them aggressive beggars and can spread disease.
animals.didYouKnow: Rock squirrels are excellent climbers and often raid low branches in the historic orchards.
